t: The Etymological Tapestry of Hacker Culture: From FOO to RISC-V
s: This article explores the linguistic evolution of core computing terms like 'foo,' 'bug,' 'patch,' 'grok,' and 'cruft,' tracing their diverse origins from military slang and comic strips to early engineering and sci-fi. It highlights the pivotal role of pioneering hacker communities like MIT's TMRC in shaping this vocabulary and its connection to the broader trajectory of open-source hardware and the embedded computing revolution, culminating towards RISC-V.
sub: Dual etymology of 'foo' from comic strips & military FUBAR, converging at MIT TMRC.
Origins of 'bug' (Edison, Hopper) and 'patch' (physical tape repair) in engineering.
Hacker culture adoption of 'grok' (Heinlein's Sci-Fi) & 'cruft' (MIT jargon).
MIT's Tech Model Railroad Club as a crucible for early hacker language and practices.
Raspberry Pi's impact on embedded systems and the shift towards open-source hardware like RISC-V.
